entries.title: In CPS win, Jessica Biggs’ took precincts across the city but her coattails were not long, data shows
entries.summary: <p>Chicago chose its first fully elected school board on Nov. 3, with voters picking the Chicago Teachers Union-backed candidates for 10 of 20 board seats, with one still close to call, and for president, Jessica Biggs, with the support of anti-CTU forces.</p><p>After expensive campaigns where voters were pummeled with mailers, digital ads and, for the president’s race, incessant negative commercials, a Sun-Times and WBEZ analysis of Chicago Board of Election voter data shows how the winning candidates managed to rack up the votes.</p><p>Biggs, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" target="_blank" ><u>who won with 49% of the vote</u></a>, did best in majority white areas where fewer families send their children to public school. But she also outdid her two opponents in predominately Black areas, though she didn’t get a majority of votes.</p><p>Despite her decisive win, Biggs’ dominance in some voting precincts did not rub off on school board candidates that were also supported by political groups that opposed the teachers union, the analysis shows.</p><p>Keep reading to learn more about what the voter data says about where candidates came up short, where winners got their support, and what the data says about their mandate.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-2f0000" name="html-embed-module-2f0000"></a><figure class="elex-map-embed"> <h3 class="elex-map-title">Chicago school board president results by precinct</h3> <iframe src="https://kcinbk.github.io/chicago_election2026/" title="Map of Chicago school board president election results by precinct" loading="lazy"> </iframe> <figcaption class="elex-map-credit"> <span><b>Source:</b> <a href="https://chicagoelections.gov" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Chicago Board of Election Commissioners</a></span> <span><b>Graphic and analysis:</b> Keenan Chen/Chicago Sun-Times</span> </figcaption> </figure> <style> .elex-map-embed { width: 100%; max-width: 1000px; margin: 24px auto; padding: 0; } .elex-map-title { font-family: var(--font-2) !important; font-size: 26px !important; line-height: 1.15; letter-spacing: 0; color: #000; margin: 0 0 16px; padding: 0; } .elex-map-embed iframe { display: block; width: 100%; height: 650px; border: 0; } .elex-map-credit { font-family: "Proxima Nova", sans-serif; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.6; color: #000; margin: 16px 0 0; padding: 0; } .elex-map-credit span { display: block; } .elex-map-credit b { font-weight: 700; } .elex-map-credit a { color: #000; text-decoration: underline; } @media (max-width: 600px) { .elex-map-title { font-size: 22px; } .elex-map-embed iframe { height: 520px; } } </style> </div> </div><p>By Election Day, three of five of the original candidates were still in the running for school board president. Jessica Biggs, an incumbent and former Chicago Public Schools principal, beat out Hilario Dominguez, CTU’s former deputy political director, and prominent defense attorney Victor Henderson. Sendhil Revuluri withdrew from the race after ballots had already been printed.</p><p>About 86% of the more than 790,000 Chicagoans who voted this fall cast a ballot in the school board president's race. That’s a little shy of the 94% who voted for Cook County Board president. About 83% participated in the school board district races, including five uncontested contests.</p><p>Biggs’ main pitch was that she is a consensus builder who could cut through conflicts and move an agenda forward. She also said she would bring together city and state leaders to create a financial stability plan for the district that includes showing “that CPS can spend responsibly before asking them to invest more.”</p><p>During and after the campaign, Biggs boasted about her broad coalition of support that included the union that represents CPS support staff, as well as several former city and school district leaders who worked under former Mayor Rahm Emanuel. She also took $1 million from billionaire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" target="_blank" ><u>Michael Sacks,</u></a> who advised Emanuel.</p><p>Biggs was helped by the fact that an anti-CTU political group called Common Ground Collective spent more than $3.5 million million to oppose Dominguez. That group, along with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center, a centrist pro-school choice group, were united in an effort to wrest control of the school board from the CTU. Union-backed candidates, which, by virtue of having a former CTU organizer elected mayor, held the majority of the mayoral-appointed seats for the past two years in addition to winning several elected seats in 2024.</p><p>Biggs did particularly well on the North and Far Northwest sides, where voter turnout was high and people voted overwhelmingly for Biggs.</p><p>In these areas, which include the wealthy Lincoln Park area and more grassroot liberal areas in Rogers Park, Biggs got more votes than both her opponents combined.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-920000" name="html-embed-module-920000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30901069"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30901069/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Biggs, who said she wasn’t going to raise property taxes to the limit — the one measure the board currently has to increase revenue — performed at her peak in majority White areas where fewer families send their children to public schools, voter data shows.</p><p>But in parts of the South Side, West Side and majority Latino neighborhoods on the Northwest Side, Dominguez and Henderson combined got more votes than Biggs. Dominguez, who is Latino, alone got almost half of all votes in majority Latino neighborhoods.</p><p>Yet Henderson, who is Black, did not dominate in predominantly Black areas. He only got about 30% of the votes in these areas, compared to 47% for Biggs, who is white, and 21% for Dominguez.</p><p>Black voters may have favored Biggs because, as a former teacher and principal who was serving on the board, had the most experience in the education system, said Rufus Williams, a former school board president under Mayor Richard M. Daley and a host on WVON, a radio station that caters to Chicago’s Black community.</p><p>Williams said he thinks some Black voters were wary of Dominguez’ close relationship with the CTU, especially because of the role the board president will have in negotiating a contract with the union.</p><p>Also, Biggs had the money to get her name out there. Williams notes that Che “Rhymefest” Smith, a Hip-Hop artist who is Black and ran unopposed in the district that includes Woodlawn and Hyde Park, was featured in commercials on WVON touting Biggs.</p><p>“I think those things matter,” Williams said.</p><p>But CTU President Stacy Davis Gates attributed Biggs’ win to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" >big money that flooded TV</a> with negative ads about Dominguez. These ads focused on half truths about unsubstantiated allegations and whether taxes were paid on a family property.</p><p>“They put on the table a million dollars not to debate whether or not the rich should pay their fair share, not to debate whether or not Black children deserve a fully funded school with libraries,” Gates said on election night. “They spent a million dollars a week to try and lie on people. They cannot win the argument, which is why they didn't have the argument.”</p><p>Jackson Potter, vice president of the CTU, adds that Biggs’ messaging was “strategically ambiguous,” as she seemed to get behind some of the ideas promoted by CTU, such as quality neighborhood schools and an expansion of early childhood education. Only when pressed, he argued, did Biggs talk about how she was open to closing schools or fiscal responsibility, which can translate into cutting staff.</p><p>He also said some of the heavy focus on defeating Dominguez might have resulted in CTU candidates on the district level having an easier time.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d70000" name="html-embed-module-d70000"></a><div class="cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper"> <div class="cpm-gfx-embed"> <div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/30936782"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30936782/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> <div class="cpm-gfx-embed"> <div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/30937302"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30937302/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div> <figcaption class="elex-map-credit"> <span><b>Notes:</b> "No CTU and anti-CTU match-up" refers to a race where a candidate ran unopposed or where only one camp (CTU or anti-CTU) backed a candidate. District 10a had a CTU-backed candidate but she was a write-in and was not on the ballot. Write-in candidate totals have not been fully released.</span> <br> <span><b>Graphic and analysis:</b> Keenan Chen/Chicago Sun-Times</span> </figcaption> </figure> <style> .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper { align-items: start; display: flex; flex-direction: row; gap: 2rem; } .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper .cpm-gfx-embed { flex: 1; min-width: 18rem; } @media screen and (max-width: 30rem) { .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper { align-items: stretch; flex-direction: column; gap: 0; } } </style> </div> </div><p>In some areas, Biggs dominance in the president’s race did not translate into school board candidates backed by the same anti-CTU interests also doing well. In the 10 school board districts where Biggs was the top vote-getter, six candidates supported by the teachers union or the political group that funded it, Our Schools, were victorious. The candidate supported by anti-CTU forces only won four times.</p><p>The CTU/Our Schools candidates dubbed themselves “public school champions” and pledged not to close schools and instead demand that the state come through with more money to fund schools. They also supported broader ideas, including expanding universal pre-school to three-year-olds.</p><p>The CTU and Our Schools <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" target="_blank" ><u>spent significantly less money</u></a> than Common Ground Collective and the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. Those are the two major spenders in the anti-CTU camp. Common Ground Collective and The Urban Center made official endorsements in district races. While they did not endorse in the president’s race, the super PACs connected to Common Ground Collective and INCS spent money attacking Dominguez.</p><p>Despite being outspent, the CTU-endorsed candidates were able to capture half of the 20 school board district seats, with one additional seat <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-6a-results" target="_blank" ><u>still too close to call</u></a>. Their candidates did particularly well in Latino areas and in areas with more than 75% of children enrolled in public schools, voter data shows.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6f0000" name="html-embed-module-6f0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30902837"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30902837/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Six races were not included in the Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis because those contests didn’t feature a CTU-backed candidate against an anti-CTU candidate.</p><p>The anti-CTU forces claimed all of those school board seats, including five that were uncontested, giving their numbers a big lift<b>. </b></p><p>In three school districts, two incumbents and one newcomer were kicked off the ballot through petition challenges. The Urban Center, one of the anti-CTU groups, hired lawyers to successfully pursue those challenges.</p><p>And in other two districts, only the incumbent board members, both of whom typically vote with the anti-CTU block, filed petitions to get on the ballot. Both were ultimately re-elected.</p><p>The anti-CTU forces argue that the fact that CTU didn’t run candidates in these races was a failure on the union’s part, with the executive director of Common Ground Collective writing in Crain’s Chicago Business that “the vaunted CTU political operation stunningly stumbled out of the gate.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Chicago School Board election results</b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-99ebbb22-d88c-11f1-a0f8-2966deb425a8"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-results" target="_blank" >What you need to know about all 21 races</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" target="_blank" >Political groups spent $12 million to defeat CTU candidates. One losing race cost $76 per vote.</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-teachers-union-poised-to-capture-half-of-school-board-district-seats-but-likely-to-lose-presidency" target="_blank" >CTU poised to capture half of school board district seats, but loses president’s race</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" target="_blank" >Jessica Biggs wins president race</a></li></ul></div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Keenan Chen

entries.title: Chicago animal rights activist is sentenced to jail time after falsely reporting shooting at 'backyard rodeo'
entries.summary: <p>A longtime animal rights activist in Chicago was sentenced to 60 days in jail, 60 hours of community service and a year of probation after being found guilty of hounding dispatchers downstate and making a false report of a shooting with the aim of getting police sent to a “backyard rodeo” where she believes livestock were being mistreated.</p><p>North Side resident Jodie Wiederkehr, 57, was sentenced this month by Ogle County Judge Anthony Peska after a jury found her guilty of a felony and a misdemeanor. With "day-for-day" good-behavior credit, the 60-day sentence would translate into 30 days.</p><p>Backyard rodeos have been held in rural and semi-rural locales in Illinois in recent years, including some suburban sites.</p><p>The rodeos often include an event called “steer tailing,” which involves someone on horseback chasing down a fleeing steer and wrapping a leg around the animal’s tail, with the intent of it tumbling to the ground. Beyond injuries from the fall, the steers sometimes have their tails ripped free in the process, something called “degloving.”</p><p>Animal rights activists have been trying to halt the practice, arguing it violates the state’s animal cruelty statute, though some say the wording is too vague to prosecute under. There have been unsuccessful legislative efforts to refine the law to more explicitly bar steer tailing statewide, while some county governments are also taking it on.</p><p>Wiederkehr — a member of SHARK, which stands for SHowing Animals Respect and Kindness — said she was remotely monitoring one of the rodeos being held last year in the Rochelle area west of DeKalb, “getting the play-by-play from the field team that was there” monitoring the event via drone.</p><p>“There were steers being degloved, overworked, criminally abused,” she said.</p><p>She said she called the Ogle County sheriff’s non-emergency number numerous times and, frustrated and angry that nobody was going to be sent, ultimately told a dispatcher there was a shooting in an attempt to force a police response.</p><p>There had been no shooting, and Wiederkehr said she regrets saying that, and is embarrassed, but in the moment was “distraught.”</p><p>“Two steers and a horse got legs broken at a previous rodeo there,” she said.</p><p>She insisted she “didn’t harass” the dispatchers, saying that “each time I called there was a crime happening” that amounted to animal cruelty, but wasn’t taken seriously.</p><p>Her attorneys asked for no jail time.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Peska said in court that after reading character letters about Wiederkehr it's clear she's viewed as “a coveted family member, friend, advocate,” according to a transcript.</p><p>Even so, he said it’s important to impose a sentence serving as a deterrent.</p><p>“I think it's of critical importance to realize we’re not in a county with unlimited resources,” Peska said. “When you call the Ogle County sheriff’s department, they might have two deputies on duty for the entire county,” so a bogus call can take them away from a legitimate emergency.</p><p>Wiederkehr argued that, while she made a mistake, the sheriff’s office did not really believe there’d been a shooting, and that she was prosecuted because Ogle County State’s Attorney Mike Rock was angry about Wiederkehr previously criticizing him over a lack of prosecutions involving the rodeos.</p><p>Wiederkehr’s lawyers filed court papers portraying this as a “vindictive prosecution.”</p><p>The judge rejected that argument, and Rock said it’s not true.</p><p>“Our prosecution, in every case, is to pursue justice, and that’s what was done here,” Rock said. “She wasn’t treated worse or better because of who she was . . . she committed a criminal act and we pursued it.”</p><p>“I did believe jail was appropriate,” Rock added, noting the statute allowed a prison sentence on the felony of up to three years.</p><p>Chris Carraway, one of Wiederkehr’s attorneys, said Peska previously has gone lighter on more serious offenses, including an incident in which a teenager threatened to "shoot up" a school and got 24 months of probation.</p><p>Peska wouldn’t let Wiederkehr present a defense based on the argument “that I broke the law to prevent a greater harm,” she said. Nor would the judge let the jury see video of the rodeo in which animals were mistreated, Carraway said.</p><p>Rock said “they wanted to turn this into a week-long trial of whether steer tailing is appropriate or not when the issue was whether she made repeated calls and ultimately a false report of a criminal offense.”</p><p>An appeal on the sentence, conviction or both is expected.</p><p>Under pressure, organizers of the Ogle County rodeo have stopped holding the event.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/05/suburban-backyard-rodeos-steer-tailing-animal-cruelty" target="_blank" >Suburban backyard rodeos under fire, with steers knocked down, sometimes stripped of their tails</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/18/mchenry-county-judge-acquits-backyard-rodeo-steer-woodstock" target="_blank" >Man who kicked a steer in its head at suburban backyard rodeo acquitted on animal cruelty charge</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Review: Chicago Shakes’ ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’
entries.summary: <p>In October, Chicago Shakespeare Theatre opened its production of “The Winter’s Tale,” and now, running in repertory with that high-quality but uneven production, we have an even better, intensely physical, quite rip-roaring “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” with the same director (the theater’s leader Edward Hall), elegantly bare set (from designer Michael Pavelka), and cast, along with an extremely similar opening framing device.</p><p>This isn’t exactly a traditional repertory approach familiar to Shakespearean companies in England and elsewhere (the Oregon and Stratford Shakespeare Festivals, for example). Those generally involve engaging an ensemble for an entire season of plays, but the productions themselves don’t necessarily have direct relationships to each other beyond sharing casts.</p><p>These two shows, though, weren’t just cast together but clearly conceptualized simultaneously. They come across as fraternal twins offering a unifying take on Shakespeare as a creator of fantasy.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Jan. 3<br><b>Where:</b> Chicago Shakespeare Theater, 800 E. Grand Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $65-$125<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoshakes.com/" target="_blank" >chicagoshakes.com</a><br><b>Run time:</b> 2 hour and 20 minutes with one intermission</div> </div><p>Hall begins both productions with a bed and a character reading a children’s book, which emphasizes innocence, playfulness and imagination. It’s not the seasonal references of the titles — “Winter” and “Midsummer” — that jump out with this choice, but the storytelling qualities of “Tale” and “Dream.”</p><p>In “Midsummer,” the storybook is presented by the impish Puck, played with proper joyous mischievousness by Patty Roache. Roache also sets the physical bar for the show by performing impressive gymnastic moves on hanging ribbons for Puck’s first monologue, an emblem of the magical nature of the fairy world, led by the elaborately garbed Oberon (Sean Fortunato) and Titania (Jessica Dean Turner). The servant fairies pop through a surprising number of trapdoors, dressed in ruffled white collars, pointed clown hats and masks, like figures out of <i>commedia dell’arte</i>.</p><p>The Oberon-Titania scenes here have a certain emotional restraint, but that certainly isn’t true of the core lover scenes. From their first entrance, the four romantic leads bound about with chaotic energy to match the nature of their oversized and inconstant emotions. Lysander (Dan Haller) and Demetrius (Esteban Ortiz-Villacorta) are both over the moon for Hermia (Felicia Oduh), and then for her oft-self-deprecating friend Helena (Grace Steckler), all thanks to Puck’s anarchic interventions.</p><p>Once the confusion begins, it’s all intense fun, with two special contributions particularly worth mentioning: Steckler provides the sincerity that also makes us care about how it ends, and fight and intimacy choreographer Zev Steinrock enables these talented young actors to throw themselves at and onto each other with an extremely effective sense of abandon. That’s difficult, and rare. And very funny. I was certainly surprised by the level of physicality that continued even when the actors entered the audience.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Dressed in Edwardian music-hall tweeds, these players are led by two ensemble members who stand out across both shows. Chiké Johnson lends an inner touch of noble confidence from his kingly character in “The Winter’s Tale,” and adds a perpetual smile to the big-egoed and much-abused Bottom here, making him as endearing as he is ridiculous. And Erik Hellman, as Quince, shows us (again!) how subtle excellent acting can be, and how simple, sharp lucidity can make supporting characters feel essential. In a show that’s an enviable embarrassment of comic riches, Hellman provides perhaps the most ideal, meta moment of all in the very meta “Midsummer” when he experiences a momentary actor’s nightmare once the spotlight hits.</p><p>On occasion, I thought the show sacrificed too much human vulnerability for performative preening, particularly with the lovers. But it requires a lot of careful self-control to make a show feel this physically urgent, and the overripe qualities of the lovers ended up coming across as purposeful. At the end we’re watching them, whom we’ve been laughing at for their oversized absurdity, make fun of the mechanicals’ oversized absurdity. That element — their condescension as an obvious show of self-blindness — works here in a way I haven’t seen before. This is certainly a superior production of one of Shakespeare’s most delightful plays.</p><p>In the end, the artist whose work most shines through the combination of productions is not an actor at all, but Pavelka, whose costume designs have a notable continuity — the refined use of black and white, the pops of rock-star leather and glamour contrasted with threads of nostalgia. Within all the eclecticism, there’s clarity, a clear reference to multiple performance traditions and on occasion, assisted by Marcus Doshi’s lighting, an extravagant beauty that’s quite extraordinary.</p><p>It’s the design work in these shows that connects them into a single, Shakespearean fantasy.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Chicago’s Japanese garden has a long history that almost disappeared
entries.summary: <p>This summer, after visiting the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park, I walked over to the Osaka Garden across the street. It was my first time seeing the tranquil garden and its manicured paths, small wooden bridge and fish pond. I had learned about it last year after writing a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/08/02/world-war-ii-america-japan-nuclear-war-hiroshima-nagasaki-amy-yee" target="_blank" ><u>column</u></a> about the 80th anniversary of the nuclear bombings in Japan.</p><p>One Curious City listener wanted to know if the garden was around during the 1893 World’s Fair.</p><p>It turns out its origins do date back to the Columbian Exposition, and the garden has lived several lives. It was burned down after World War II due to anti-Japanese hostility. It nearly disappeared as weeds and brush took over the unkempt land. But in recent decades, it was revived. Today, people like me are discovering the garden for the first time as they visit the Obama Center.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure But most of the work that he found was dishwashing and working in Asian food restaurants.”</p><p>In 1946, the Phoenix Pavilion burned in an arson attack. Months later, a second fire destroyed most of it.</p><p>Over the years, the site became overgrown and wild, and it seemed like the garden was lost. But like a phoenix, it did rise from the ashes.</p><h3><b>Revival of the garden</b></h3><p>In 1973, Chicago and the Japanese city of Osaka became sister cities. The Chicago Park District and community groups started to revive the garden. It reopened in 1981, but it was not as vibrant as it is today.</p><p>Then in the 1990s, support for the garden grew and cultural events were organized. understanding at the 1893 World's Fair,” Karr explained.</p><p>Skylanding especially reflects Ono’s work as a peace activist. In 2016, she spoke at its dedication in Chicago. “I'm working on the world peace, and I really think that we can make it,” Ono said.</p><h3><b>A cultural touchstone</b></h3><p>Today, the garden is what original caretaker Shoji Osato intended: a bridge between cultures. Michael Tanimura, chair of the Chicago Japanese American Council, first visited the Osaka Garden about 15 years ago. It’s become part of his Japanese American identity, realized only as an adult. When he was growing up in Chicago in the 1950s and 1960s, he just wanted to blend in as American.</p><p>Tanimura didn’t know much about his parents’ incarceration during World War II because they didn’t talk about it. “I never really thought to ask why, because it just was how things were and then I just accepted it,” he said.</p><p>In the 1990s, Tanimura learned more about their experience when his daughter interviewed his parents and relatives for a middle school project. “Even after knowing these things, I wasn't allowed to ask any questions of them,” he said.</p><div entries.title: As religious identities change in America, a Berwyn mosque welcomes growing Latino Muslim community
entries.summary: <p>A once-shuttered church in Berwyn is now home to a growing community of Latino Muslims.</p><p>For years, Latino converts to Islam in the Chicago area struggled to find religious spaces and support networks that reflected both their faith and their cultural backgrounds.</p><p>That includes Raul Gonzalez, who grew up Pentecostal in Humboldt Park and converted to Islam 26 years ago. </p><p>“Islam talks about the unity of the believers, and so I was looking for more brothers, more people like myself, Latino Muslim converts,” he said. </p><p>Then he met Christopher AbdulKareem Pavlicek, who felt the same way, and they started looking for a space where Spanish-speaking Muslims could gather.</p><p>They found it in Berwyn, in that shuttered church. </p><p>"So we needed to come together, and just really to establish something, and stop being guests, and start becoming hosts," Pavlicek said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Islamic Center at 1900 S. Oak Park Ave. in Berwyn.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In February, on the first day of Ramadan, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2026/03/05/latino-muslims-ojala-islamic-center" target="_blank" >Ojala Islamic Center opened in Berwyn as the Midwest’s first Latino-led mosque</a>, offering converts a place to practice Islam while maintaining ties to their cultural heritage. Pavlicek is its founder and serves as imam.</p><p>“I was searching for a community for a long time,” Pavlicek said. “Nobody's doing it. I have to do it myself."</p><p>The mosque opened amid a shifting religious landscape. <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2026/11/18/the-future-of-world-religions-population-growth-projections-2020-2070/" target="_blank" >New Pew Research Center projections</a> released Wednesday show the Muslim population in North America is expected to more than triple, from about 6 million people in 2020 to 20 million by 2070. In the United States, the Muslim population is projected to grow by about 9 million, reaching roughly 4% of the country's population.</p><p> Illinois has the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/race-class-communities/2022/07/28/illinois-has-the-most-muslims-per-capita-in-the-us " target="_blank" >nation’s highest concentration of Muslims per capita</a>, according to a 2022 study by the Institute for Social Policy and Understanding and the University of Illinois Chicago. More than 350,000 Illinoisans identify as Muslim, mostly residing in the Chicago area. About 8% of the state's Muslim population is Hispanic, the study found.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6a0000" name="image-6a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7625039/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/578f03a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b4bd89/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Raul Gonzalez at the Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn. Oak Park Ave. in Berwyn, which opened earlier this year.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ahmed Rehab, executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations' Chicago chapter, said he's seeing the most rapid Muslim growth among young women and Latino converts.</p><p>“A lot of Muslims don't know that Latinos are the fastest-growing community,” he said. “When you learn that, they're surprised themselves.”</p><p>Pew projects that migration and natural population growth will drive much of Islam's expansion in North America. Muslims' relatively young population and higher birth rates are also contributing to growth, according to Pew research. </p><p>But immigration and birth rates tell only part of the story. At Ojala, many members were raised in other faiths before converting to Islam after coming to the United States and exploring their own spiritual identities.</p><p>Pavlicek said the congregation is as much “convert-led” as it is “Latino-led,” with much of its community made up of people from different religious and cultural backgrounds who are embracing Islam for the first time.</p><p>Nelson Julio-Polanco, born in the Dominican Republic and raised Catholic, found a sense of belonging at Ojala, which offers services in Arabic, English and Spanish. As the only Muslim in his family, Julio-Polanco said speaking Spanish with other Muslims made the community especially welcoming.</p><p>“When they founded this organization, I felt like, wow, I can speak Spanish to these people and they're Muslims too,” he said. “We have the same culture.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Nelson Julio-Polanco, who is of Dominican heritage, was happy to find other Spanish-speaking Muslims at the Ojala Islamic Center at 1900 S. Oak Park Ave. in Berwyn.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>After four years as a practicing Muslim, Julio-Polanco is making the pilgrimage to Mecca for the first time Friday.</p><p> Catholicism remains deeply woven into the cultural identity of many Berwyn neighborhoods, particularly Latino communities. The Catholic Church also is growing : 1,059 adults became Catholic in Chicago during this year's Easter season, a 52% increase from the previous year, said the Archdiocese of Chicago in <a class="Link" href="http://archchicago.org/about-us/ocia" target="_blank" ><u>its study</u></a> of the recent surge in adult conversions to the church.</p><p>For Pavlicek, Ojala is not about replacing that legacy but creating space for another faith community within it.</p><p>“We're filling a void,” he said. “We're sitting in the building that was created as a church.”</p><p>Before becoming a mosque, the building at 1900 S. Oak Park Ave. served as First Reformed Church of Berwyn <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/ojala-foundation-and-making-space-for-chicagolands-latino-muslim-communities/" target="_blank" >for 77 years,</a> according to the Chicago History Museum.</p><p>The transition reflects a practical convergence, Rehab said. Some churches with shrinking congregations are looking to sell their buildings, while a growing Muslim population needs space. </p><p>Rehab sees the mosque as part of Chicago's religious history, not a departure from it.</p><p>“It's sort of a win-win on both ends,” he said. “Muslims appreciate and even embrace the Catholic legacy of Chicago, which lives on. We're contributing our own touch to the painting.”</p><p>In Berwyn, Pavlicek said worshippers like himself travel long distances to attend Ojala, the only mosque within a six-mile radius. As the congregation grows, he said, Ojala is already looking to establish another Islamic center in Pilsen to serve more Chicagoans. </p><p>Karen Rios, Pavlicek's wife and mother of their two children, said the mosque is where her religious and cultural identities can coexist. Raised Catholic in Mexico City, she came to Chicago to study to become an au pair but decided to stay, she said, to practice her Muslim faith freely in her community.</p><p>“I wanted to pray almost every day here, like to stay with the community, so that's why it was also part of my choice to stay here,” she said. “To practice my religion.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Let the Bears' offensive line — the Monsters of the Midsection — lead the way
entries.summary: <p>Three things I think I know about the 7-2 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, who gulped down the last of their bye-week umbrella drinks, plucked the cucumber slices from their eyes, stuffed their freshly pedicured feet back into their cleats and shall re-take the gridiron Sunday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nfl/2026/11/15/bears-next-opponent-saints-fall-to-the-panthers-20-17" target="_blank" >against the Saints at Soldier Field</a>:</p><p><b>1. They need the Monsters of the Midsection to take over: </b>Since the Bears’ offensive extravaganza in the opener at Carolina, when they rushed for 291 yards on a slicing-and-dicing 7.5 yards per carry, they’ve not exceeded 4.3 yards per carry in a game and have failed to average four yards six times. That’s two more sub-four games than the Bears had all last season, when they ranked third in the NFL in rushing. They’re fourth — but slipping — now.</p><p>Yes, running back Kyle Monangai’s expected return after a five-game injury absence should give the running game an instant jolt. No doubt, coach Ben Johnson made good use of the bye scheming in his X’s-and-O’s lair underneath an invisible North Shore mountain.</p><p>But this is about the big fellas up front, people. The wall o’ beef. The belly bumpers. Indeed, the Monsters of the Midsection. Without them leading the way, good stuff won’t happen.</p><p>“It always starts up front with us,” guard Jonah Jackson said. “It has to.”</p><p>The Bears run the ball more often than any other team and have a chance against the Saints’ soft run defense to have the sort of gash-happy game that could set a tone for the rest of the season. At Halas Hall during the week, the offensive linemen were all but counting down the hours to Sunday’s first collision.</p><p>“If it’s our time to step up to the plate, I hope we step up and I think we will,” tackle Darnell Wright said. “Yeah, I’m pretty sure about that.”</p><p>Said Jackson, “Maybe things aren’t as pretty as they were last year at points, but I don’t have any doubt in my mind that it’ll come to life — and maybe even more [than last year].”</p><p>The Bears seemingly downgraded at center from Drew Dalman to Garrett Bradbury, but they’re in good enough shape across the line to go on a good run. Make that a lot of good runs.</p><p>“When those guys are on point, my job’s easy,” Monangai said. “I’m serious, it’s easy. They’re that good. That’s why I know we’re going to be back to it real soon.”</p><p><b>2. Their rabbit act is working: </b>Nobody gets out faster than the Bears, the NFL’s highest-scoring team in the first quarter at 8.4 points a pop. In a highly related development, quarterback Caleb Williams leads the league in first-quarter completion rate (78.3%) and passer rating (130.3). Johnson’s script work is strong.</p><p>The Bears aren’t keeping it up for 60 minutes — they’re tied for 17th in second-quarter scoring, sixth in the third and 25th in the fourth — so there’s room for improvement. But the fast starts are why their games are so much less stressful than they were last season, when Williams and the offense often seemed incapable of kicking into gear until they’d given Bears fans ulcers. This way is a lot better.</p><p><b>3. Williams needs a clean sheet: </b>As in no interceptions against the Saints after his four-INT implosion — talk about stressful — in the Bears’ last game, a narrow win against the Buccaneers. The worst thing to find out would be that Williams’ sudden case of the giveaways wasn’t just a weird one-off. Crazy but true: Even after that brutal night, he has the lowest career interception rate — 1.36% of his passes — of any QB with at least 1,000 attempts in NFL history. (No. 2 on the list: some dude named Aaron Rodgers.)</p><h3><b>Confidence-o-meter: 9 out of 10</b></h3><p>“We are very confident,” linebacker Devin Bush said.</p><p>“We are confident in who we are,” Williams said.</p><p>“This team? Very confident,” Jackson said.</p><p>One almost gets the feeling these Bears aren’t racked with doubt. Almost.</p><h3><b>Look who’s coming: the Saints</b></h3><p>The danger begins with defensive ends Chase Young, a former No. 2 overall pick, and Carl Granderson, a former undrafted free agent. Both grizzled veterans by now, they’ve combined for 16½ sacks.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Bovino murder plot fights deportation</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-d/" target="_blank" >Jon Seidel</a></h5><p><b>In custody</b>: Ten months have passed since Juan Espinoza Martinez, 38, heard the words "not guilty" — but he's still not a free man. Immigration authorities have held the Little Village resident in custody since he was acquitted of plotting the murder of then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, the controversial face of the Trump administration's<a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-h/" target="_blank" > Midway Blitz deportation campaign</a>.</p><p><b>Sun-Times interview</b>: In a call arranged by his legal team, Espinoza Martinez said he'd rather sit behind bars than be deported without his loved ones to Mexico, a country he doesn't remember. Espinoza Martinez said he was brought to the U.S. as a child, and today, his children, siblings and mother all live in Chicago. "I'm not abandoning my family," Espinoza Martinez said. "I'm going to hold on, incarcerated, because I'm not giving up."</p><p><b>Key context</b>: His fight for freedom has now stretched more than a year, starting when federal authorities <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-k/" target="_blank" >accused him of soliciting Bovino’s murder</a>. Espinoza Martinez put his fate in the hands of a jury, in the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-u/" target="_blank" >only trial to result from Operation Midway Blitz</a>. The panel swiftly acquitted him in January, deliberating for about three hours. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-o/" target="_blank" >took him into custody</a> the next day. He is now being held in Missouri, ICE records show.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-b/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>HOUSING their bills change wildly each month as more landlords turn to a "ratio utility billing system," known as RUBS. It's estimated that tens of thousands of Chicago renters live in buildings that use RUBS.</p><p><b>How it works</b>: A landlord will outsource the billing to a third-party company like Conservice, which splits up the master gas, sewer and water bills according to a formula based on the size of the apartment, the number of occupants, and other factors. Conservice then tacks on a service fee and sends the bill out to renters.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: Consumer advocates and tenant organizations say this way of billing is becoming more of a trend in master-metered apartment buildings that don't have separate water and gas meters for each unit. Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering the state's plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change, a pair of recently released state reports found.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: Under an ambitious law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. But big new data centers are requiring so much electricity that it has become difficult for the state to shut down all of the coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand, the reports found.</p><p><b>Bottom line</b>: The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year. Hank Fiene is your man.</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-ty/" target="_blank" >Neil Steinberg</a></h5><p>Hank Fiene scrapes a wire brush across an enormous slice of cheesecake.</p><p>Or, rather, across a triangular wooden frame covered in plywood, then encased in sheets of Styrofoam, which Fiene is transforming into a wedge of Eli's cherry cheesecake eight feet long and four feet tall, rotating on a circular platform on a float in the parade at the Wintrust Magnificent Mile Lights Festival this Saturday.</p><p>"This float has to be done by Thursday morning," says Fiene, coated in tiny bits of polystyrene, standing in the cluttered, sprawling warehouse of ABC Parade Floats in Ashburn.</p><p>"There used to be eight parade float companies in the Chicagoland area," he says. "There are only two of us left in the Midwest now."</p><p>Fiene, who started ABC in 1990, supplies floats to about 70 parades a year.</p><p>Growing up on the South Side, Fiene dreamed of being a portrait artist, then "found out you have to die before you can make any money," he says. So he shifted to the idea of being a commercial artist. "But you need a lot of experience for that." So he went into the parade float business as a teenager, and still marvels at his good fortune.</p><p>"I'm always amazed I make a living doing this," he says. "C'mon, I build parade floats."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-tj/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>LET’S HEAR FROM YOU 🗣️</h4><p>Now that the midterm election dust has just about all cleared, we want to hear about what you thought of our coverage.</p><p>We'd like to know what helped, what was missing and what we could do better next time.</p><p><b>Take our five-minute survey </b><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkrljlk-l-ti/" target="_blank" ><b>here</b></a>.</p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition! entries.title: Blackhawks need Patrick Kane's newfound rhythm to carry them without Connor Bedard
entries.summary: <p>Patrick Kane has looked like a rejuvenated player since returning from the upper-body injury that cost him a week of action.</p><p>Did the rest do him some good? Perhaps. But it seems Kane did some deep thinking and self-assessing during his week apart from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>, too. He has returned to the lineup with a few logs added to his fire.</p><p>"It sucks missing games and being out of the lineup, and it's not fun watching even more so when the team's losing," Kane said Monday. "Coming back, [I'm] trying to make sure I'm ready to play, make sure I'm competing at a high level and trying to create.</p><p>"Sometimes you play a certain way for your whole career, and then all of a sudden, you play with some different players and it's a different game. You've got to change it up a little bit. [I'm] just finding my game a little bit more."</p><p>Presuming Connor Bedard will miss time as a result of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/17/connor-bedard-injured-blackhawks-maple-leafs" >his injury Tuesday</a> — the Hawks are expected to provide an update after practice Wednesday — Kane will need to really drive the team's offense moving forward. So his newfound rhythm is well-timed.</p><p>That rhythm has come on a line with Frank Nazar and Oliver Moore, two forwards who certainly play different styles. While Kane has historically relied on vision and stickhandling to slow the game down, Nazar and Moore are blazers who try to speed it up as much as possible.</p><p>Nevertheless, their combination has developed some chemistry. During the 61 minutes they've spent together during five-on-five play, the Hawks have generated a 36-22 advantage in shots on goal and 32-29 advantage in scoring chances (per Natural Stat Trick), although goals are just 3-3.</p><p>"I'm trying to use their assets to my advantage, too," Kane said. "How can I use their speed to create chances?</p><p>"Frank, he's getting a breakaway every game just from his speed, so how can we maximize that asset we have on our line? Same thing with Moore: he's a great skater. He's able to stop on a dime, turn up, make plays on his backhand, things like that. [We're] just talking through it and trying to figure out the best way we can play."</p><p>For whatever reason, Kane hasn't <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/19/blackhawks-patrick-kane-nine-games-connor-bedard-roman-kantserov" target="_blank" >clicked</a> the same with Bedard — at least at five-on-five. The Hawks have been outshot 33-29 and outscored 4-3 during their time together.</p><p>And when Kane has played apart from both Bedard and Nazar, the Hawks have been slaughtered: 46-20 in shots and 7-1 in goals.</p><h3><b>Moving faster</b></h3><p>Those goal ratios should improve once Kane's shooting luck turns. His last 32 shots on goal — dating back to the season opener — have all been saved. That streak won't last forever.</p><p>Whether through scoring or playmaking, though, the Hawks desperately need Kane to help maintain the offensive momentum they built Tuesday. As he approaches his 38th birthday Thursday, he has 11 points (10 of them assists) in 18 games so far this season.</p><p>It remains to be seen how Bedard's injury will affect the Hawks' forward lines, but it would make sense to keep Kane, Nazar and Moore together regardless.</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill said Kane communicates well with coaches and teammates and regularly brings up his own clever ideas, including one recently about a specific way Moore could use his speed.</p><p>"Kane does a good job of getting pucks off the wall in his breakouts," Blashill said. "Then...there's just so much speed. If he can put pucks in the right areas for those guys, they’re going to stress the defense."</p><p>Kane appears to be moving faster lately, as well. He was clocked at 21.98 mph on a tenacious backcheck during overtime last Thursday against the Sabres — his second-fastest recorded speed in three seasons — and he blew past Jets defenders for an eye-opening rush chance Saturday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Kane wheels in for a shot: <a href="https://t.co/oj6JygHC01">pic.twitter.com/oj6JygHC01</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2121722390518595878?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Kane joked that he's simply hoping to "keep up with" Nazar and Moore.</p><p>"I made...an area play out of the zone [Saturday], not expecting anything and going to get a change," Moore said. "And you just see him flying up the wing. I’m like, 'Holy [crap], wow!' He obviously takes care of himself."</p><h3><b>Also a teacher</b></h3><p>Kane's ability to opine intelligently and eloquently about any hockey-related subject thrown at him is remarkable. It's a testament to how much he loves and closely he follows the sport.</p><p>Before the Sabres game, for example, Kane analyzed in detail the Sabres' 8-3 loss to the Lightning that he had watched the night before. Then on Monday, Kane spoke at length about Maple Leafs rookie Gavin McKenna.</p><p>His enormous knowledge base has proved useful and helpful for the Hawks' coaching staff.</p><p>"I've always thought you can learn a lot from your top players, especially someone who’s been through as much as he’s been through," Blashill said. "So [I've been] just having conversations with him. Sometimes he may look at things a little bit different than the way you look at them, and it makes you a better coach because of it."</p><p>Moore has also learned a lot from playing with Kane.</p><p>"Every shift you learn something playing with him, honestly," Moore said. "There’s times when I get back to the bench and he's like, 'You had more time than you thought there.' You watch it back on film, and you're like, 'I had way more time than I thought there.' And he’s processing that throughout the game. He [has], obviously, an elite mind."</p>

entries.title: Recent ground stop shows need to privatize air traffic control
entries.summary: <p>In the wake of the nationwide ground stop, all accusatory fingers are being pointed. Democrats argued that Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy is woefully inexperienced. Duffy and the MAGA administration countered by saying that Congress has not appropriated sufficient funds to modernize the Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system.</p><p>The truth about the failures lies elsewhere. The fundamental problem is that the government is in charge of these matters. Sound economic theory points that it would be much better handled by the private free market. And that’s not just theory. In Canada, for example, Nav Canada, a privately funded company, manages air traffic control. Canadian air travel appears to be more efficient, modern and less accident-prone than ours.</p><p>This example provides clear evidence that the received “wisdom” of both the Dems and MAGA that air control can best (and perhaps only) be handled by the government is fallacious.</p><p>The simple solution is to privatize air traffic control.</p><p><i>William P. Gottschalk, Lake Forest</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-560000" name="module-560000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Best woman for the job</h3><p>If Mayor Brandon Johnson has an open, logical mind, he should choose Antoinette Ursitti as the next Chicago police superintendent. She is young, talented and seems to have the backing of City Hall and an eye for details, leadership and the ability to listen, which is essential in Chicago. The others have talent and ability but not the grit and street smarts that are an asset in Chicago. Hopefully, the mayor works with all concerned parties and does the right thing.</p><p><i>Richard J. White, Elmhurst</i></p><h3>Tap youth to discuss Meta settlement allocation </h3><p>Social media has been a part of my world for as long as I can remember. My friends and I have never known life without it. We’ve experienced the good parts, like sending videos to our friends at night, knowing they’re awake too. But we’ve also seen how something that can bring us together can make us feel isolated and insecure.</p><p>The harms caused by social media aren’t anecdotal for us. They’re real. We see and feel them. That’s why youth deserve a seat at the table about where the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/technology/2026/08/26/meta-illinois-pay-nearly-768-million-multistate-settlement-teen-social-media-addiction" >Meta settlement dollars</a> are going in Illinois.</p><p>Our state will receive nearly $768 million over the next 10 years. I'm glad to know the money may go toward <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/illinois-is-getting-a-piece-of-metas-proposed-17b-settlement-wheres-the-money-going/3980812/" target="_blank" >after-school programs</a> and other initiatives, but the youth must be part of the conversation.</p><p>I’ve learned firsthand why our voices matter. As a former member of Boston Children’s Hospital’s Student Advisory Council for Digital Wellness, I shared my voice with representatives from Instagram, Roblox and other companies shaping young people’s online lives. Along with other teens, I advocated for platform-level reform and integrated time management. Advocating for those without a voice felt like telling my younger, voiceless self that he could change the world. I also learned that change requires other teens willing to share their experiences with cyberbullying and mental health challenges.</p><p>In addition, I've learned how investing in young people can be transformative. After-school programs aren’t just places to pass the time. They’ve helped me grow into adulthood, whether by buying my little brother an Oreo McFlurry on a hot summer day or learning to shop for my family’s groceries. Joining the After School Matters' Orleans Leadership Council was a declaration that I was more than a student — I was a doer and a leader. Writing papers without a grade and advocating for Ukrainian Village’s culture after gentrification proved that I had the power to shape my community and future.</p><p>I can’t change the world my generation grew up in. But I want to help shape what comes next. I’ve seen what happens when we give young people a voice, and I know what happens when policymakers invest in our potential.</p><p><i>Mason Kelly, junior, Whitney Young</i></p><h3>State grant also helps educate veterans </h3><p>Hats off to Logan McMullen for his recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/11/11/veterans-educational-opportunities-trump-midterms-measles-sexual-assault-house-speaker-blackhawks" >letter</a> about informing veterans about educational opportunities. I was drafted in 1970, and upon my return, I used the GI Bill to attend Chicago's Northeastern University, where I got my undergraduate degree in economics. That degree led to a wonderful lifelong government job where I retired after 35 years. I often wonder what kind of job I would have gotten without the GI Bill.</p><p>That said, I want to alert our Illinois veterans of yet another source of assistance for school — the <a class="Link" href="https://veterans.illinois.gov/services-benefits/education/illinois-veterans-grant.html" target="_blank" >Illinois Veteran Grant</a> that covers full tuition and most fees for any community college or state university in Illinois. The federal school benefit, the Forever GI bill, has no <a class="Link" href="https://www.va.gov/resources/compare-va-education-benefits/" target="_blank" >expiration</a> if you separated from active duty on or after Jan. 1, 2013. The state grant is similar.</p><p>Veterans seeking more information about the Illinois Veteran Grant should contact the Illinois Department of Veterans Affairs at 800-437-9824 or <a class="Link" href="http://veterans.illinois.gov/" target="_blank" >veterans.illinois.gov</a>.</p><p>And to all the veterans who may read my letter, thank you for your service.<br> <br><i>Ray Toczek, service officer, American Legion Post 183, Portage Park</i></p><h3>Practice what you preach</h3><p>To the 11 Democrats who couldn’t be bothered to vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth:</p><p>The blue tsunami only happened because your constituents took the time to vote.</p><p>At the very least, you could do the same.</p><p><i>Glen Moore, Oak Park</i></p><h3>Mascot musings </h3><p>So, Sun-Times reader Chet Alexander thinks the symbol of the GOP is a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/11/11/veterans-educational-opportunities-trump-midterms-measles-sexual-assault-house-speaker-blackhawks" >white elephant</a>?</p><p>But what is the symbol of his party? A jackass!</p><p><i>Robert E. Frey, West Ridge</i> <br></p>

entries.title: Fred Mitchell, former Tribune sportswriter, dies at 78
entries.summary: <p>Fred Mitchell, the former Tribune columnist and sportswriter who covered the Bears, Bulls and Cubs, died Tuesday after a three-year battle with leukemia. He was 78.</p><p>Mitchell was with the Tribune from 1974 to 2015. He also wrote 12 books and is the namesake for the award given to the top college kicker among more than 750 non-FBS schools. </p><p>In 2023, he was inducted into both the Chicagoland Sports Hall of Fame, and he received the Chicago Headline Club's Lifetime Achievement Award the next year. After retiring from the Tribune, Mitchell was an adjunct professor at Northwestern and DePaul.</p><p>Mitchell is survived by his wife of 25 years, Kim, and their son, Cameron, 23.</p>

entries.title: La Policía de Chicago rara vez confisca las armas de agresores domésticos, pese a ley estatal
entries.summary: <p>Cuando su exnovio abusivo le apuntó con un arma a la cabeza este verano, Dominique dijo que supo que tenía que hacer algo antes de que fuera demasiado tarde.</p><p>Así que acudió a la corte y solicitó una orden de protección para mantener a su ex alejado y una orden de cateo para que la policía fuera a recuperar su arma. Pudo hacerlo amparada en la Ley de Karina, una ley de Illinois que entró en vigor el año pasado con la intención de proteger a las sobrevivientes de violencia doméstica.</p><p>"Sólo no quiero morir", dijo la joven de 26 años a un juez de la Corte del Condado de Cook.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-900000" name="module-900000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Sus solicitudes fueron concedidas, y un juez le dio al Departamento de Policía de Chicago 96 horas para ejecutar la orden. Pero eso no ocurrió. En su lugar, un policía convenció al juez de anular la orden dos días después.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/05/12/ley-de-violencia-domestica-nombrada-en-memoria-de-karina-gonzalez-entra-en-vigor" target="_blank" >Desde que la ley entró en vigor el año pasado</a>, la Policía de Chicago ha adoptado este enfoque ante casi todas las órdenes de registro ordenadas por la corte destinadas a recuperar las armas de presuntos agresores, según halló una investigación del Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>En 91 casos, los jueces emitieron órdenes según la Ley de Karina que instruyen a la policía a incautar armas de fuego, muestran los registros.</p><p>Sólo en tres ocasiones la policía de Chicago lo hizo.</p><p>Cuando la policía ejecutó esas órdenes de registro e incautación, se recuperaron armas en cada ocasión. En un caso, se hallaron 26 armas de fuego en una vivienda.</p><p>Maralea Negrón pasó años presionando a los legisladores de Illinois para aprobar la Ley de Karina.</p><p>"Ver que está fallando en lugares donde se concedió una orden de registro —un documento legal muy serio y una directiva de un juez— es muy desalentador y socava por completo la intención de lo que tratamos de lograr con la aprobación de la Ley de Karina", dice Negrón, quien es vicepresidenta ejecutiva de políticas e impacto de The Network: Advocating Against Domestic Violence.</p><p>La policía dice que no están cumpliendo las órdenes de ir a las casas de los agresores y confiscar sus armas por preocupaciones de seguridad tanto para sus oficiales como para los dueños de las armas.</p><p>"Nuestro enfoque es recuperar armas de agresores en casos de violencia doméstica de la manera más segura posible para todas las personas involucradas", dice un portavoz del departamento, y añade que algunas armas sí se incautan durante arrestos o cuando los presuntos agresores las entregan voluntariamente después de emitida una orden.</p><p>Dominique, que accedió a ser entrevistada con la condición de que sólo se la identificara por su nombre porque teme por su seguridad, cuestiona cuándo la policía "se lo tomará en serio".</p><p>"¿Qué se necesitaría?", pregunta. "¿Tendría que ocurrirme algún daño o un incidente fatal? Dios no lo quiera".</p><h3>Preguntas sobre el sistema de honor</h3><p>La Ley de Karina fue la culminación de una batalla legislativa de años sobre cómo endurecer las medidas contra los agresores que poseen armas. Entró en vigor en todo el estado el 11 de mayo de 2025 —el Día de las Madres estadounidense.</p><p>La ley lleva el nombre de Karina González, quien fue asesinada a tiros en julio de 2023, semanas después de decir a la policía que su esposo, José Álvarez, la había amenazado. Su hija de 15 años, Daniela, también fue asesinada.</p><p>A González le habían concedido una orden de protección que le prohibía a Álvarez poseer un arma. Pero su arma nunca fue retirada.</p><p>En aquel entonces, las sobrevivientes de violencia doméstica podían solicitar que retiraran las armas cuando pedían una orden de protección. Pero sus defensoras dicen que la aplicación de la ley era inconsistente y a menudo insuficiente.</p><p>La Ley de Karina se presentó como una solución. Ahora, los jueces que conceden una orden de protección también pueden emitir una orden de registro e incautación de armas para las fuerzas del orden.</p><p>Si la sobreviviente ha hecho recientemente una denuncia policial, los agentes tienen 96 horas para ejecutar la orden. Si no, la policía tiene 48 horas para investigar y plantear cualquier objeción ante un juez.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-53ce78" name="image-53ce78"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8ce19b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/380a192/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8980e8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Un memorial para la residente de Little Village Karina González y su hija de 15 años, Daniela, en 2611 S. Millard Ave., el 13 de julio de 2023. Fueron baleadas y asesinadas en julio de 2023 por el esposo de Karina, dos semanas después de que Karina había recibido una orden de protección de la corte que debió haber llevado a la incautación del arma de fuego que poseía su esposo." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8980e8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2e106c8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8980e8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F09%2Ff0%2F0e2deea6d601e1e4cb4b6eed2933%2Flittlevillage-07xx23-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Un memorial por la residente de La Villita asesinada, Karina González, y su hija de 15 años, Daniela, en julio de 2023. Fueron baleadas y asesinadas en julio de 2023 por el esposo de Karina, dos semanas después de que Karina había recibido una orden de protección de la corte que debió haber llevado a la incautación del arma de fuego que poseía su esposo.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Owen Ziliak/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Las preguntas sobre cómo se ha implementado la ley surgieron después de que un funcionario de la Policía de Chicago compareciera ante la Junta del Condado de Cook a fines de marzo.</p><p>Mike Milstein, subdirector de la Oficina de Servicios a Víctimas del departamento de policía, reconoció que la policía había ejecutado apenas dos de las 60 órdenes de la Ley de Karina que se habían emitido hasta ese momento. Milstein les dijo a los comisionados que algunas personas objeto de esas órdenes de cateo entregaron voluntariamente sus armas, por lo que no fue necesario realizar los registros.</p><p>Eso encendió "una gran señal de alarma" para Benna Crawford, abogada directora de Legal Aid Chicago, que ofrece representación gratuita a quienes no pueden pagar un abogado.</p><p>"Intentar quitarles las armas a los demandados mediante el sistema de honor y la entrega voluntaria es exactamente el sistema fallido que la Ley de Karina se aprobó para corregir", dice Crawford.</p><div class="Enhancement" Cuando no está en la escuela, cuenta, pasa la mayor parte del tiempo en casa con su hijo pequeño.</p><p>"Tengo el deber de proteger a mi hijo aunque tenga miedo por mí", dice. "Es una sensación muy desconcertante. Tengo que poner cara valiente. Tengo que mantener la cabeza en alto. Pero no puedo dejar que mi lluvia moje a mi hijo".</p><p>La orden de protección de Dominique aún no ha sido notificada.</p><p>"A las víctimas de violencia doméstica, sean hombres o mujeres, solo quiero que el sistema nos reconozca y luche por nosotros", dice.</p><p>Manny Álvarez, el hijo de Karina González, ha estado impulsando cambios desde que mataron a su madre y a su hermana.
