entries.title: Blackhawks star Connor Bedard dealing with new shoulder injury: report
entries.summary: <p>For a second consecutive year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> star Connor Bedard has injured his right shoulder on a faceoff.</p><p>The injury Bedard <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/17/connor-bedard-injured-blackhawks-maple-leafs" >suffered Tuesday</a> against the Maple Leafs was indeed to his shoulder, ESPN's Emily Kaplan reported Wednesday, even though the point of contact was to his hand.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">This is the best replay of the Connor Bedard injury: <a href="https://t.co/5nDMy0ScE5">pic.twitter.com/5nDMy0ScE5</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2122884824767586645?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>It's the same shoulder Bedard injured on a faceoff last December against the Blues. He decided not to undergo surgery in that instance and eventually returned after missing 12 games over about a month.</p><p>It's not the same shoulder Bedard had surgery on this past July after a fluke injury in a summer scrimmage. That was his left shoulder, which has seemingly held up fine this season. It took him a little over three months to recover from that surgery.</p><p>Hawks coach Jeff Blashill is expected to provide an official update on Bedard's status after the team finishes practice (around 12:30 p.m.).</p><p><i>This story will be updated.</i></p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Illinois Republicans stick with General Assembly leaders McCombie, Curran after steep election losses
entries.summary: <p>SPRINGFIELD — Two weeks after a brutal election that shrunk their caucuses to historically small sizes, General Assembly Republicans voted to stick with their leaders as the party seeks a path back to relevance in reliably blue Illinois.</p><p>House Minority Leader Tony McCombie, R-Savanna, fended off a challenge from state Rep. Regan Deering of Decatur during a Tuesday night caucus vote in the Capitol, earning McCombie a third term spearheading political and legislative efforts in a chamber that has weathered frequent intra-party squabbles.</p><p>Senate Minority Leader John Curran, R-Downers Grove — the only Chicago-area Republican left in his chamber — won his third term after Channahon state Sen. Chris Balkema dropped a challenge he had initially mounted on the assertion that “a defensive strategy is not a winning strategy.”</p><p>Democrats flipped several seats Nov. 3 to bolster already-massive supermajorities in Springfield, which will balloon to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/blue-tsunami-democrats-massive-advantage-illinois-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>the largest in modern history</u></a> when members of 105th General Assembly take the oath in January.</p><p>Pending certification of election results, they were on track for an 84-34 edge in the House and 45-14 in the Senate, up from 78-40 and 40-19.</p><p>Republicans have been hamstrung in Illinois by President Donald Trump’s unpopularity in the vote-rich Chicago area, not to mention a starkly gerrymandered, Democrat-drawn political map that’s up for redistricting in four years.</p><p>It’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/20/bob-grogan-illinois-republican-party-new-chairperson-dupage-county-auditor" target="_blank" ><u>often led to infighting</u></a> as downstate, hardline conservative General Assembly members chafe against their more moderate leaders.</p><p>“The vote made clear that members want a more united caucus,” McCombie said in a statement. “I value hearing what my colleagues think, and I look forward to working with Rep. Regan Deering to bring our caucus together.</p><p>“We all came here to serve the people who sent us to Springfield. We do better when every member uses their voice to work together on the issues that matter to Illinois families,” said McCombie, who won the leadership vote 20-13, with one colleague voting "present."</p><p>Curran called it “a hard election for our party, and our caucus had an honest conversation about what comes next.”</p><p>“Open debate makes a caucus stronger, and every member will have a voice in the work ahead,” he said in a statement. “Since Election Day, I have talked with many of our members about how we rebuild. They have brought forward constructive ideas, especially the members of my leadership team, and I am committed to putting those ideas to work. That work starts now.</p><p>“Illinois families are paying more and getting less under one-party rule in Springfield. They deserve an effective opposition and a real alternative. Senate Republicans will be both,” Curran said.</p><h3><b>Democrats reelect Harmon, jockey for Welch’s post</b></h3><p>There was no such tension for Illinois Senate President Don Harmon, who faced no opposition for reelection Tuesday to the post he’s held since 2020.</p><p>But House Democrats were just ramping up the race to succeed House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside, who announced he’d give up the gavel after losing support amid complaints over his delayed response to sexual harassment allegations against ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield.</p><p>Chairs in the caucus have laid out a flexible timeline asking candidates to officially throw their hats in the ring this week, make their cases to colleagues during the second week of the fall veto session Dec. 1-3, and then vote on their next leader during the lame-duck session in January.</p><p>Numerous <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/06/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-steps-down-female-replacement-contenders" target="_blank" ><u>names are being floated</u></a>, including Chicago Democrats Eva-Dina Delgado, Kam Buckner, Marcus Evans and Ann Williams, as well as Jehan Gordon-Booth of Peoria and Jay Hoffman of Swansea, near St. Louis. More are expected to join the fray.</p><p>“I’m confident any one of my current leaders is prepared to step up and become our next speaker because leadership requires leaders to prepare the next leaders,” Welch said in a statement Wednesday. “In two months, let’s all unite to support our new speaker whoever that may be.”</p><h3><b>Easing into veto session</b></h3><p>The legislative wheels slowly started turning with Tuesday’s kickoff of the fall veto session, with all eyes on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/11/16/bears-stadium-bill-illinois-lawmakers-fall-veto-session-house-speaker-replacement-data-centers" target="_blank" ><u>the push for a Bears stadium bill</u></a>.</p><p>Negotiations were ongoing behind closed doors. Buckner and state Sen. Bill Cunningham, his fellow Chicago Dem running point on talks in his chamber, have said they hope to get a municipal stadium authority bill over the goal line by Dec. 3, but the drive could end up lingering until January.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s top adviser, Jason Lee, was in the Capitol for talks with legislators and lobbyists in the city’s bid to keep the Bears in Chicago.</p><p>The stadium authority model would pit the city against Arlington Heights to woo the Bears with a publicly owned stadium. Lee said they’re generally on board with the idea, and confident in any of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/11/12/michael-reese-hospital-developers-10-billion-stadium-bears" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago proposals</u></a> floated by developers in recent weeks, though City Hall hasn’t endorsed a specific vision.</p><p>“There are several places in the city that could serve a world-class stadium, but there is only one city that maximizes the return for the team and the state of Illinois, and that’s Chicago,” Lee said.</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Hombre de Chicago absuelto de complot contra Gregory Bovino lucha contra su deportación
entries.summary: <p>Han pasado diez meses desde que Juan Espinoza Martínez oyó las palabras “no culpable”, pero aún no es un hombre libre.</p><p>El Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) ha mantenido al residente de La Villita detenido desde que fue absuelto de conspirar para asesinar al entonces comandante de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Gregory Bovino, la controvertida cara de la audaz campaña de deportaciones Operativo Midway Blitz del gobierno de Trump en el área de Chicago.</p><p>En una llamada organizada por su equipo legal esta semana, Espinoza Martínez dijo que prefiere permanecer tras las rejas antes que ser deportado a un país que no recuerda, sin sus seres queridos.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2e0000" name="module-2e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“No voy a abandonar a mi familia”, Espinoza Martínez dijo al Chicago Sun-Times. “Voy a intentarlo con todas mis fuerzas. Voy a aguantar, encarcelado, porque no me voy a rendir”.</p><p>Su lucha por la libertad ya se extiende más de un año, desde que las autoridades federales lo acusaron de haber solicitado el asesinato de Bovino.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez puso su destino en manos de un jurado, en el único juicio que surgió del Operativo Midway Blitz. El panel lo absolvió rápidamente en enero, deliberando apenas unas tres horas.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Y ahora se encuentra detenido en la Cárcel del Condado de Greene en Missouri, según registros de ICE.</p><p>ICE no quiso hacer comentarios cuando fue contactado el martes. El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) no respondió.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez, de 38 años, dijo que llegó a Estados Unidos cuando era un niño pequeño. Un juez lo describió como ciudadano mexicano que ingresó a Estados Unidos siendo menor de edad, hace más de 30 años, “sin inspección ni admisión legal”.</p><p>Su caso es otro ejemplo llamativo del daño que provoca cuando los fiscales presentan cargos de alto perfil que no se sostienen en la corte.</p><p>No sólo los federales acusaron a Espinoza Martínez del plan de asesinato, los registros judiciales lo identificaron como “miembro de rango de los Latin Kings”. Los abogados defensores de Espinoza Martínez, Jonathan Bedi y Dena Singer, negaron que tuviera alguna afiliación con pandillas o antecedentes penales.</p><p>Bedi dijo que su cliente “trabajó constantemente para mantener a su familia mientras contribuía positivamente a la comunidad” e incluso ayudaba a entrenar a los equipos deportivos de sus hijos.</p><p>Los fiscales finalmente retrocedieron en su afirmación sobre los Latin Kings. Eso llevó a que un juez prohibiera el testimonio relacionado con pandillas en el juicio. Y una semana después, el jurado declaró a Espinoza Martínez no culpable en uno de varios enjuiciamientos de Midway Blitz que se derrumbaron en la Corte Federal Dirksen de Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b011fd" name="image-b011fd"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7be7083/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3899x2188+0+124/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2Fcf%2F91de849c1dcee65dbb61f47565a7%2Fdirksen.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c46a15e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3899x2188+0+124/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2Fcf%2F91de849c1dcee65dbb61f47565a7%2Fdirksen.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1a7314d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3899x2188+0+124/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2Fcf%2F91de849c1dcee65dbb61f47565a7%2Fdirksen.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="La Corte Federal Dirksen, en el 219 S. Dearborn St.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Archivo Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Allí los federales acusaron a 33 acusados conocidos de delitos vinculados al operativo. Pero los cargos contra 28 de ellos han sido retirados. Y los fiscales ahora están bajo escrutinio por presunta mala conducta en un caso fallido contra un grupo de manifestantes de ICE conocido como los “Broadview Six.”</p><p>Espinoza Martínez dice que se está “aguantando” en Missouri. Pero la odisea ha sido dura para él y su familia.</p><p>Su hermano menor, Oscar Martínez, destacó los cumpleaños y días festivos que han pasado sin él. “Somos una familia que siempre estuvo unida”, dijo Oscar Martínez en una entrevista.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez es padre de tres hijos y dijo que tiene oportunidades regulares para hablar con su familia. Pero contó que su hijo menor, que apenas tiene 4 años, no comprende plenamente por qué su padre no está en casa.</p><p>“Le miento un poco”, reconoció Espinoza Martínez, señalando que le dice al niño que está “trabajando lejos de casa”.</p><p>Pero su hijo aún se queja, “Te estás tardando mucho”.</p><h3>Vínculos profundos con Chicago</h3><p>Espinoza Martínez tiene 38 años. Y pasó tres décadas en Estados Unidos, señalan sus simpatizantes.</p><p>“Toda su vida, su familia, sus hijos, sus hermanos y su madre viven en Chicago”, dijo un abogado a un juez en febrero.</p><p>Lo han descrito como carpintero afiliado a un sindicato. Dijo que incluso trabajó en el recién inaugurado Centro Presidencial Obama en el lado sur de Chicago.</p><p>“Durante la última década ha trabajado en la empresa constructora de su hermano, presentándose todos los días para ganarse la vida honestamente”, escribió el abogado Michael Adler en un documento judicial el pasado invierno, pidiendo la liberación de Espinoza Martínez. “Nunca ha sido condenado por un delito. Nunca ha dado motivo a nadie para dudar de su carácter.</p><p>“Antes de esto, el señor Espinoza Martínez era simplemente un hombre trabajador con profundas raíces en su comunidad, yendo a trabajar y llevando a sus hijos a sus partidos de fútbol”.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez dijo que ni siquiera se dio cuenta de que estaba en Estados Unidos de forma irregular hasta que llegó a la secundaria. Contó que sus padres siempre trabajaron y pagaron sus impuestos, por lo que nadie esperaba problemas.</p><p>Los registros judiciales muestran que Espinoza Martínez incluso participó en el programa de Acción Diferida para los Llegados en la Infancia (DACA). Oscar Martínez dijo que una vez intentó ayudar a su hermano a obtener estatus legal, pero le dijeron que el proceso podría tardar 25 años.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez dijo que en México le espera poco. No tienen familia allí, afirmó su hermano.</p><p>“He estado aquí desde que tenía 3 años”, dijo Espinoza Martínez. “No tengo recuerdos de allá, en absoluto”.</p><h3>El juicio</h3><p>Los federales formularon cargos penales contra Espinoza Martínez un mes después del inicio de Midway Blitz. La noticia llegó cuando el presidente Donald Trump intentaba desplegar tropas de la Guardia Nacional en Chicago, con miembros de su administración quejándose de amenazas a agentes federales.</p><p>Los fiscales federales acusaron a Espinoza Martínez de ofrecer $10,000 por el asesinato del entonces jefe de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Bovino. Señalaron un mensaje de Snapchat que Espinoza Martínez envió a alguien a principios de octubre.</p><p>El mensaje seguía de una foto de Bovino.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Pero los abogados solicitaron un juicio rápido, en cambio. Un juez empezó a seleccionar los miembros del jurado el 20 de enero, menos de cuatro meses después de que se presentaran los cargos.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez dijo que estaba “muy asustado”.</p><p>“No sabía qué pensar”, dijo. “Estaba temblando. Pareció contener la emoción por un momento, aunque levantó brevemente la mirada al techo.</p><p>“Me sentí muy bien”, dijo Espinoza Martínez. “Y al mismo tiempo, sentí mucha tristeza. Porque supe que justo después de eso, tenía que venir aquí”.</p><p>La jueza federal Joan Lefkow pronto emitió una orden que decía que Espinoza Martínez “deberá ser liberado tan pronto como sea práctico después del trámite correspondiente”.</p><p>Pero a la hora de salir del Metropolitan Correctional Center alrededor de las 6 a.m. al día siguiente, dijo, “ICE ya me estaba esperando”.</p><h3>Esperando un alivio</h3><p>Los federales inicialmente llevaron a Espinoza Martínez al Condado de Clay, Indiana. Más tarde lo trasladaron a Missouri. Un juez de inmigración le negó la fianza a Espinoza Martínez en febrero, calificándolo de “posible” peligro para la comunidad.</p><p>La decisión se produjo menos de un mes después del veredicto del jurado.</p><p>Ahora, el caso de Espinoza Martínez está ante la Junta de Apelaciones de Inmigración, donde aún podría tardar meses en resolverse. Así lo indicó un portavoz del Centro Nacional de Justicia para Inmigrantes, que lo está ayudando con el caso.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez dijo al Sun-Times que ha tenido “una vida dura por ser inmigrante”. Pero, añadió, su encarcelamiento ha sido “lo peor”.</p><p>Los titulares que salieron sobre él el año pasado “me afectaron mucho”, dijo. La gente se lo ha preguntado en la cárcel. Y, dijo, “mi hija empezó a ver todo eso también”.</p><p>Aun así, mostró su agradecimiento por la forma en que su comunidad respondió y ayudó a cuidar de sus hijos. Dijo que está listo para “dejar lo que pasó en las noticias en el pasado”.</p><p>Dijo que toma las cosas “un día a la vez”, esperando noticias de la Corte de Inmigración.</p><p>Y esperando oír estas palabras por el altavoz: “Juan Espinoza Martínez, te vas a casa”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: City Council urges Springfield to put a 'millionaire tax' on the ballot
entries.summary: <p>Amid accusations of political “hypocrisy,” the Chicago City Council unanimously approved a resolution Wednesday urging the Ilinois General Assembly to put a binding amendment to the state constitution on the ballot authorizing a tax on individual income over $1 million.</p><p>Members of the renegade faction that rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax last year and have vowed to do it again this year were accused of talking out of both sides of their mouths by introducing the resolution.</p><p>Johnson's Council supporters, while backing the resolution, said it also leaves the dirty work of taxing the rich to Springfield while the Council continues to do the opposite at home.</p><p>“I am at a loss right now trying to wrap my head around the hypocrisy of this introduction from people who have been completely opposed to taxing the rich and are passing the buck to the state,” said Ald. Rosanna Rodriguez-Sanchez (33rd), one of Johnson’s most outspoken Council supporters.</p><p>“It is wild to me that we have literally a budget proposal that calls for taxing wealthy corporations in Chicago. … This is an opportunistic attempt to brand themselves as progressive without actually having to do it.”</p><p>Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez (25th) said "the hypocrisy is just laughable" — and guffawed for emphasis.</p><p>“You cannot keep opposing things without proposing an alternative. You keep protecting rich and powerful individuals,” Sigcho-Lopez said, uging his colleagues to “leave the theater and the theatrics out of this” and put their political muscle where their mouths are. </p><p>"Who’s gonna go to Springfield now that we are so courageous? ... Let’s put action into this resolution,” Sigcho-Lopez said.</p><p>Ald. Michelle Harris (8th) countered that the millionaires tax and Johnson’s attempt to revive his failed head tax — at a monthly rate of $25-per-employee for businesses with more than 125 workers — are very different things.</p><p>“Taxes on jobs is a killer. It will kill our economy. It will kill our city. And it’s the fastest way to get big businesses to leave our city, take their jobs, run away and take them to communities all outside the city,” Harris said.</p><p></p><p>Zoning Committee Chair Gilbert Villegas (36th) said the Council’s “hands are tied. … We do need Springfield to help us out here.”</p><p>He said the millionaires’ tax resolution “outlines concrete action items to get the wealthy to pay their fair share” unlike the tax-the-rich “rhetoric” from Johnson with nothing to show for it.</p><p>Twenty-eight alderpersons have declared they oppose more than $400 million of the mayor’s tax-the-rich ideas, including the revived head tax.</p><p>Johnson has challenged critics to present revenue-raising alternatives to the tax increases they don’t like — even though they claim the onus is on him.</p><p>With that in mind, Ald. Jesse Fuentes (26th) urged her colleagues to cool it with the political finger-pointing.</p><p>“This is an easy vote. … But, I want to caution us throwing daggers at each other at this moment,” Fuentes said.</p><p>“We need each other to pass this budget. We got some budget woes — and they’ll be worse next year. And so, while I believe in the progressive revenue in the proposed budget, I’m not gonna shoot an arrow at the folks that are skeptical right now."</p>

entries.title: City Council mandates that city redeploy gunshot detection technology
entries.summary: <p>More than 72% of Chicago voters want to bring back gunshot detection technology to fight violent crime and speed emergency response times to gunshot victims.</p><p>On Wednesday, a defiant City Council responded to that advisory Nov. 3 referendum by lighting a political fire under Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration.</p><p>By a 43 to 7 vote, alderpersons approved an ordinance that gives Chief Procurement Officer Sharla Roberts 30 days to finalize the new gunshot detection contract that Johnson promised more than two years ago but has failed to deliver.</p><p>If a replacement for the technology once provided by ShotSpotter is not in place within 60 days, Roberts must provide the Council’s Committee on Contracting Equity and Oversight with a written explanation for the delay.</p><p>"Our commissioner, hopefully is listening, who has ... the authority to move this thing along and not play games with the procurement process," said Ald. Anthony Beale (9th), one of Johnson's most outspoken City Council critics. </p><p>"Because we all know this was being stonewalled and prolonged and delayed. We know the script. But the time to act is now ... The people have spoken in volume to turn this technology back on while we're waiting for the pilot that will probably never materialize."</p><p>West Side Ald. Emma Mitts (37th) said 82% of her constituents voted to bring back gunshot detection technology.</p><p>"We asked and they answered. Now, it's our turn," Mitts said. "Every minute counts. If somebody gets shot and nobody calls 911, an alert can help police and paramedics get there sooner."</p><p>Mitts noted the City Council voted twice to keep ShotSpotter, but the system was turned off anyway.</p><p>"Nine companies put in a bid by April of last year. Nineteen months later, we still don't have a contract. What are we waiting on? Let's finish this job," Mitts said.</p><p>"When we bring it back, I want us to start in the districts with the most shootings. Don't make people wait on another test."</p><p>Ald. David Moore (17th) has been among ShotSpotter's chief proponents. Nevertheless, he voted against the ordinance, saying he wanted to avoid a legal battle.</p><p>"We cannot force ... the procurement officer to select a vendor in 30 days when the process is not complete," Moore said.</p><p>"I'm not comfortable doing that while we're in the middle of a process. If this ordinance said turn ShotSpotter on until we find someone, I'd be the first one to say yes."</p><p>In February 2024, Johnson honored a campaign promise to progressive supporters by canceling the contract with ShotSpotter, technology he derisively called a “walkie-talkie on a stick.”</p><p>Johnson and his supporters viewed the technology as costly, ineffective and a contributor to overpolicing in Black and Brown communities where the majority of gun violence occurs.</p><p>Even so, the mayor did negotiate a costly extension to retain the technology through the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago.</p><p>The Council also at one point empowered then-Chicago Police Supt. Larry Snelling to sign a new contract with ShotSpotter, but Johnson declared that ordinance illegal. Johnson then launched an open competition to replace ShotSpotter. SoundThinking, the company that owns ShotSpotter, was one of 15 firms responding to the request for information and one of nine companies responding to a follow-up request for proposals.</p><p>Nothing has happened since then — even though the last two city budgets set aside a combined $13.9 million for the replacement technology. Another $5 million is included in Johnson’s reelection budget.</p><p>Council hearings have done nothing to pressure the mayor to deliver a replacement contract.</p><p>Roberts was a no-show at the most recent hearing. She infuriated Council members by sending a letter informing them a pilot gunshot-detection program was about to begin in six police districts: Wentworth, Calumet, Englewood, Deering, Ogden and Harrison.</p><p>When the chief procurement officer finally did make an appearance at Council budget hearings, she disclosed that the 72% vote had prompted the Johnson administration to alter the upcoming test.</p><p>Roberts said her office initially planned a pilot program with one vendor that wasn’t involved in a lengthy, competitive bidding process. But the Johnson administration has now decided to let all “short-listed” bidders, including ShotSpotter, showcase their violence prevention strategies in the pilot, Roberts said.</p><p>The mystery program still will test a variety of ideas, including more violence intervention, “drone-based situational awareness, license plate recognition and incident response systems for evidence preservation.”</p><p>Gunshot-detection technology remains only part of the pilot.</p><p>ShotSpotter proponents called the mystery test a stalling tactic to get past the mayoral election.</p><p>During a City Hall news conference Tuesday, Johnson said he has “always been in favor of gunshot detection,” but only after a field test to prove the technology will deliver crime-fighting results.</p><p>The mayor reiterated his long-standing claim that ShotSpotter “was proven to be ineffective” and failed to deliver on its promise to drive gun violence down.</p><p>“I said, 'Let’s do the responsible thing. Let’s cancel that one. Let’s open up the process so that we can actually see together as a city what actually works and then we can make a determination from there,'” he said.</p><h3>In other action</h3><p>Also on Wednesday, the City Council voted 42 to 8 to approve an order mandating the city’s Office of Public Safety Administration to audit every city vendor that “maintains manages or otherwise provides automatic license plate readers” to ensure that they are not violating privacy laws or the state law that bars information sharing with federal immigration enforcement.<br></p>

entries.title: Defiant City Council authorizes three-year review of city finances in response to CFO resignation
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration has characterized the internal dispute that triggered the resignation of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch as a “technical difference of interpretation” and “much ado about nothing.”</p><p>The Chicago City Council strongly disagrees.</p><p>That much was obvious Wednesday when a veto-proof City Council majority voted 45 to 5 to authorize an independent review of the city’s finances and financial statements to reassure Wall Street rating agencies and would-be investors shaken by the abrupt departure of Johnson’s third CFO in the last year.</p><p>It was the latest and perhaps the strongest show of force yet by a City Council that has grown more independent than ever as it capitalizes on what they see as Johnson’s political weakness.</p><p>Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th), Johnson’s most powerful Council ally, denounced the three-year review as a “waste of taxpayers’ money” and a “waste of resources.”</p><p>“We’re talking theater here. I’m trying to figure out who’s gonna get the Emmy here and who’s gonna get the Oscar,” Ervin said.</p><p>“We might be a couple million dollars short because we decided to do something we already know the answer to.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6c0000" name="image-6c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3e39a9c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2F61%2F43fa21bb4516833335ae585ac057%2Fcouncil-ervin-11-02-26.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2950b91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2F61%2F43fa21bb4516833335ae585ac057%2Fcouncil-ervin-11-02-26.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/24cbdb6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2F61%2F43fa21bb4516833335ae585ac057%2Fcouncil-ervin-11-02-26.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Jason Ervin (28th)." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/24cbdb6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2F61%2F43fa21bb4516833335ae585ac057%2Fcouncil-ervin-11-02-26.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/287a9e9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2F61%2F43fa21bb4516833335ae585ac057%2Fcouncil-ervin-11-02-26.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/24cbdb6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F52%2F61%2F43fa21bb4516833335ae585ac057%2Fcouncil-ervin-11-02-26.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Jason Ervin (28th) speaking to the City Council earlier in November.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Retiring Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) countered there is a “clear lack of transparency, accountability and confidence” in the Johnson administration after Chicago’s third chief financial officer in a year “walked out the door.”</p><p>“We need an independent review of who knew, when they knew and what they did and what they were foolish enough to put in emails or in the presence of other people about our finances,” O’Shea said.</p><p>“People are looking at us. The taxpayers, bond rating agencies. They want to know what’s going on. And we owe it to the taxpayers to lift up the hood and see what’s going on and who knew what, what they knew about it and what they did about it.”</p><p>His voice rising, O’Shea said Chicago has an acting budget director, an acting CFO and an acting corporation counsel.</p><p>“That doesn’t show stability. That shows a clown car without anybody at the driver’s wheel,” O’Shea said.</p><p>“And if you’re not concerned about the that and just as important, if you’re not concerned about the way this administration repeatedly treats women in this building in leadership roles, then you’ve got a problem.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-950000" name="image-950000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3163476/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7057x3961+0+373/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F0b%2Fdb367d26491d83c3b77a5f9809f3%2Fcouncil-260930-11-oshea.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8c71c11/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7057x3961+0+373/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F0b%2Fdb367d26491d83c3b77a5f9809f3%2Fcouncil-260930-11-oshea.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0edfa83/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7057x3961+0+373/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F0b%2Fdb367d26491d83c3b77a5f9809f3%2Fcouncil-260930-11-oshea.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Matt O'Shea (19th)" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0edfa83/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7057x3961+0+373/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F0b%2Fdb367d26491d83c3b77a5f9809f3%2Fcouncil-260930-11-oshea.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b5abc64/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7057x3961+0+373/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F0b%2Fdb367d26491d83c3b77a5f9809f3%2Fcouncil-260930-11-oshea.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0edfa83/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7057x3961+0+373/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F0b%2Fdb367d26491d83c3b77a5f9809f3%2Fcouncil-260930-11-oshea.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) at a Chicago City Council meeting in September.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The ordinance authorizes Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) to select and engage one or more independent professional services firms to conduct an “impartial and comprehensive review” to determine whether any “material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition” have been made to investors, City Council and the public in any “document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the last three years.”</p><p>Designated firms have subpoena power. City officials and employees are compelled to cooperate with the three-year investigation and provide access to all city records, reports and information requested by the designated firms, the ordinance states. Anyone who refuses to cooperate faces “employment sanctions, including suspension or discharge.”</p><p>Four years ago, Dowell broke with then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot and endorsed Johnson in what turned out to be a turning point in the 2023 mayoral campaign.</p><p>Johnson rewarded her with the Finance Committee chair, but history has repeated itself. Last year, Dowell led the budget rebellion that prompted the Council to reject Johnson’s corporate head tax. This year, she joined 27 colleagues in opposing more than $400 million of Johnson’s tax-the-rich ideas.</p><p>Wednesday’s vote was an equally important political break. The money to bankroll the financial review will be drawn from the Finance Committee’s annual budget, Dowell said.</p><p>Dowell described her support for the three-year review a "moment of angst" for her personally that "many of us share."</p><p>"Now more than ever, there are increasing eyes on the city's fiscal condition. They are all watching and we need to make sure that our math is correct," Dowell told her colleagues.</p><p>Pointing to what she called, “piecemeal emails and claims” that Gabrysch “missed meetings” and was “iced out,” Dowell said: “Where there’s smoke, there’s fire. The City Council must know the unvarnished truth.”</p><p>A former analyst for Fitch Ratings, Gabrysch resigned Friday after just three months on the job. She quit after being admonished, frozen out, and as sources closes to her said, bullied for publicly and privately contradicting the mayor’s claim that his $17.6 billion budget was 76% structurally balanced.</p><p>Gabrysch said only 56% of the moves the mayor had made to erase a $882 million shortfall were structural, because settlements tied to allegations of police abuse — and the $480 million in borrowing Johnson ordered to cover those costs — should not count as structural solutions.</p><p>At a City Hall news conference earlier this week, Johnson downplayed the conflict as a “technical” disagreement resolved by “providing both scenarios” in what he called the “spirit of full transparency.”</p><p>Acting Chief Financial Officer Michael Belsky called the disagreement “much ado about nothing,” even after Gabrysch concluded that “to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligation.”</p><p>Belsky instead argued that since the city “can issue bonds every year at any time to meet an obligation like settlements and judgments,” it is fair to say “that’s a structural match.”<br></p>

entries.title: First Wall Street fallout from CFO resignation: S&P places Chicago on CreditWatch
entries.summary: <p>Chicago on Wednesday suffered the first fallout from the abrupt resignation of the city's third chief financial officer in a year and the ongoing budget stalemate between Mayor Brandon Johnson and the City Council.</p><p>Standard & Poor’s, a Wall Street rating agency, reaffirmed its BBB rating on Chicago’s general obligation debt, but placed the city on “credit watch with negative implications.</p><p>That means there is “at least a one-in-two chance of a downgrade in the next 90 days” in a Chicago bond rating that stands just two notches above junk status depending on how the 2027 budget is and how much “progress” it makes toward “reducing the fiscal deficit.”</p><p>“The CreditWatch placement reflects or view of the elevated likelihood of a negative rating action … given the current budget stalemate and given that budget negotiations during this critical period appear to be heading down a path similar to that of the past two years, which, in our view, increases the likelihood that the city will resort to significant one-time measures to balance the fiscal 2027 budget,” the report states.</p><p>Another drop is Chicago’s already shaky bond rating is likely if the final budget “relies too heavily on unsustainable solutions to close the gap, perpetuating the city’s chronic reliance on short-term pediments that reduce fiscal resilience, the report states.</p><p>“As in the past two years, political infighting within a condensed budget timeline that allows for only roughly six more weeks of negotiations… makes an on-time budget with substantial structural enhancement difficult to achieve,” S&P said.</p><p>S&P noted that its CreditWatch action follows<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/13/ashlee-gabrysch-chief-financial-officer-resigns-chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" > last week’s abrupt resignation </a>of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch, who quit after an internal dispute about the size of the structural deficit that left her to conclude that “to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligation.”</p><p>The rating agency noted that Gabrysch’s resignation continues “a string of high-profile management departures over the past year that, at this stage, we believe constitutes a pattern of management instability that injects added uncertainty into the budget process,” the report states.</p><p>The latest spin in Johnson’s revolving door was ill-timed, to say the least.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a50000" name="image-a50000"></a> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Just days earlier, a majority of the City Council signed a letter to the mayor rejecting more than $400 million in revenue” in the mayor’s proposed $17.6 billion budget, including a $75 million up-front payment from the New York investment firm that acquired Chicago parking meters, more than $100 million from the mayor’s revived corporate head tax and $234 million from the 33% increase in the city’s tax on cloud computing and equipment leasing.</p><p>“These items aside, the corporate fund budget continues a pattern of heavy reliance on nonstructural gap-closing measures that includes bonding for legal settlements, tax increment finance fund sweeps, use of fund balance, reallocation of corporate fund expenses to other funds and a hiring freeze at the Chicago Police Department without a permanent headcount reduction,” the report states.</p><p>As a result, S&P concluded that “most of the measures” Johnson has used to close the $882 million gap in the corporate fund are “either non-structural or contested by a City Council majority.” Spending cuts are “significantly limited” in the mayor’s plan, “indicating a limited appetite for cost-cutting that further constrains the budgetary environment.”</p><p>Management turnover “adds to the city’s immediate challenges, as does the possibility that the political fallout” from Gabrysch’s resignation “will consume scarce time and attention in the weeks ahead,” S&P said.</p><p>Johnson called the warning a “sobering reminder of our collective obligation to the residents of this city” to work toward “constructive solutions” to balance the city’s pre-election budget.</p><p>"In this moment, we must come together and engage in a good-faith dialogue on behalf of all Chicagoans. It’s time to lower our voices and raise our sights," the mayor's statement said.</p><p>The mayor noted that the red flag raised by S&P "specifically cautions about the risks of an artificial gridlock as a major driver of their concern." Passing a budget would "alleviate their concerns," he said.</p><p>"S&P's warning makes clear that fiscal stability depends on the advancement of structural revenues, for that reason, it's disheartening that segments of the City Council have rejected more than $400 million in structural revenues in this year's budget," Johnson said.</p><p>The renegade group united against the mayor’s business taxes said it “sent a roadmap” to Johnson seven weeks ago “outlining a path towards collaboration on a passable budget that won’t penalize putting people to work or make everyday residents pay a 20% lease tax.”</p><p>Johnson has “done nothing” since then but “point fingers and divide” Chicagoans, the group said.<br>“This is a crisis of his own making - a one-way staring contest that threatens our city’s financial future,” the coalition said.</p><p>“Today’s CreditWatch is a a shot across the bow to the one person whose job it is to put forth a responsible, passable budget that moves all of Chicago forward and that is the Mayor.”</p><p>Acting CFO Michael Belsky said his 35 years in municipal finance lead him to conclude that the purpose of placing Chicago on CreditWatch is to elevate "market concerns" and give the city "an opportunity to remedy" those problems.</p><p>"The city can avoid a downgrade by promptly passing a balanced budget built upon structural revenue solutions," Belsky was quoted as saying.<br></p>

entries.title: Prosecutors file new terrorism charges against teen in Aurora Hindu temple shooting plot
entries.summary: <p>A Palatine teen faces new terrorism charges related to an October plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Aurora, police announced Wednesday.</p><p>Alexandros Paporakis, 19, was initially charged with making a terrorist threat and illegal gun possession, and is set to appear Thursday in Cook County court on new charges, according to a statement from Palatine police. The additional charges include six counts of terrorism, 10 counts of making a terrorist threat, two counts of armed violence, two counts of attempted terrorism, and several weapons charges.</p><p>Police arrested Paporakis on Oct. 11 as the teen left an apartment building in the 1300 block of North Baldwin Court. He had allegedly told a coworker at Taco Bell about the attempted mass shooting at the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple. The coworker then called police.</p><p>Authorities say Paporakis allegedly pulled up to the temple that morning and tried to shoot someone from his car window. But the gun jammed and Paporakis drove away, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/gun-jammed-when-neo-nazi-tried-to-commit-mass-shooting-at-hindu-temple-in-aurora-prosecutors-say" target="_blank" >authorities have said</a>. </p><p>Police searched Paporakis’ apartment and found a rifle, bullet magazines and 300 rounds of ammunition. They also found an eight-page manifesto in which Paporakis claimed to be a white supremacist, prosecutors said.</p>

entries.title: Illinois officials fear a toxic lead-dust plume may spread from Army site explosion in Iowa
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker’s top <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment" >environmental</a> official is warning that a detonation of hazardous waste at a Department of Defense site in Iowa southwest of the Quad Cities could send lead dust into the air, creating a health threat to Illinois residents.</p><p>A public notice from the federal government Monday announced that there will be a detonation of hazardous materials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, Friday between 11 a.m. and noon.</p><p>The notice describes the material designated to be exploded as “lead azide hazardous waste,” which is toxic. Lead azide is used for detonating explosives.</p><p>The explosion is expected to create a dust plume containing lead that may cross into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois" >Illinois</a>. Lead is toxic to humans and animals.</p><p>“As we witnessed during this summer’s wildfire season, air pollution does not respect state lines and accordingly we strongly urge the Department of Defense to conduct comprehensive post-detonation environmental sampling,” James Jennings, director of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency, said in a statement.</p><p>That testing, he added, should include “air, soil, and surface dust testing in potentially impacted areas of Illinois.”</p><p>Jennings asked Defense officials to share the test results with the public. The Illinois EPA will be monitoring air as well. It's unclear whether the lead dust could blow as far northeast as Chicago.</p><p>The notice from the Defense Department said it would be too dangerous to attempt to move the materials.</p><p>“The storage and treatment of this lead azide hazardous waste is in a location not covered for treatment, storage or disposal under the effective [federal environmental] permit,” according to the notice.</p><p>The Army is advising nearby residents in Iowa that there will be a plume carrying elevated levels of lead. It recommends either evacuating or avoiding the area or remaining indoors with windows closed until Army officials give an all-clear notice.</p><p>“There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health" >health</a> risks,” Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in a statement. “Illinois residents who may be affected by the detonation can stay safe by staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours. Washing your hands prior to eating and drinking, as well as washing outdoor surfaces with soap and water are ways to minimize exposure and limit the risk of tracking toxic residue into homes."</p><p>For more information on the detonation, visit the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant's <a class="Link" href="https://www.army.mil/asc#org-iowa-army-ammunition-plant" target="_blank" >public notice site</a>.</p>

entries.title: Bears' injury report: CB Kyler Gordon listed as out for practice, DT Jeffery Simmons limited
entries.summary: <p>Cornerback Kyler Gordon (shoulder) would not have practiced Wednesday and star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons (knee) would have been limited were it not for the Bears' off day.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, who are coming off a bye week, didn't practice Wednesday but instead sent out an estimated report.</p><p>Gordon, who hurt his shoulder in the team's win against the Buccaneers, left the game for the locker room but returned to finish it. He didn't participate in the Bears' light practice Monday or their padded practice Tuesday. Bears coach Ben Johnson said the team considers him day-to-day..</p><p>Simmons, for whom the Bears traded two first-round picks and a third-rounder last month, practiced Monday but sat out Tuesday. He did not have any knee issues this year with the Titans, missing practice time only with a sore back. He is expected to speak with the media after Thursday's practice.</p><p>Receiver <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/17/bears-report-luther-burden-kyler-gordon-clears-concussion-protocol-shoulder-injury-nfl" target="_blank" >Luther Burden</a> was cleared from concussion protocol and had no injury designation. Neither did running back Kyle Monangai nor cornerback Malik Muhammad, which lines all three up to play Sunday's game against the Saints at Soldier Field. Monangai hasn't played since suffering a turf toe injury in Week 4, while Muhammad last played in Week 7 because of his own toe problem.</p>
